strengths: The core model is simple and elegant: multiplying global linear coefficients by per-instance, context-dependent corrections preserves MEM = β by construction, giving a clean, well-defined notion of global interpretability that post-hoc methods cannot guarantee.

The optimization via parameter elimination is technically well developed: closed-form profiling of β, connection to adaptive ridge (with a proof of the adaptive-ridge/Lasso equivalence), re-parameterization to avoid degeneracy, extension to GLMs via IRLS, and a sub-ℓ1 generalization. The derivations are sound and complete.

The evaluation is reasonably comprehensive for the claims made: synthetic settings with ground-truth coefficients and nonlinearities, recovery of sparsity patterns, three real UCI datasets, classification extension, and an ablation on masking and positional encoding that directly validates the key design choices.

The paper is clearly written, honestly discusses limitations (e.g., inability to capture self-interactions x_j f(x_j)), and includes sufficient implementation detail in the appendix for reproducibility.
Comparison against relevant state-of-the-art interpretable baselines (LassoNet, NAM, IMN) with largely matched architectures is a fair practice.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to closely related work. The idea of instance-specific linear coefficients via deep networks is essentially the premise of the contextual lasso (Thompson et al., 2023), which the paper cites but does not compare against. The multiplicative correction form and the MEM=β property are refinements rather than a fundamentally new capability; the positioning relative to contextual lasso and IMN needs much sharper differentiation, ideally empirically.

The claim that MEM for other models 'do not yield meaningful interpretations' is overstated: MEM is computable for any differentiable model and is a standard interpretability tool. NIMO's genuine advantage is only that MEM coincides with the coefficients by construction, which should be framed more carefully.

Identifiability of β is not analyzed. Because g_j depends on x_{-j} and the joint objective is non-convex, there is a potential trade-off between the linear part and the network corrections; the recovery of true coefficients in experiments may hinge on the synthetic data exactly matching the model class. No theoretical or empirical analysis of robustness under model misspecification is provided.

Scalability of the optimization is unaddressed: each gradient step requires forming B_u and solving a d×d linear system, so the method appears limited to small/medium d and full-batch training. No runtime or memory comparison against baselines is reported.

The evaluation scope is narrow: only 200 training samples in synthetic experiments, single-run results without variance or significance tests for Table 1, and only three small/medium real datasets. Notably, NIMO does not win everywhere (LassoNet wins classification Setting 3, methods are comparable on diabetes), which tempers the performance claims.

Several key practical components are ad hoc heuristics justified only empirically: binary positional encoding of the masked index, noise injection after the first layer to 'prevent compensation', sin activations, and the group-ℓ2-on-first-layer sparsity (which the paper itself admits subsequent layers can compensate for).

The additional 'interpretability' obtained from sparsity of the first fc layer is weak: the corrections g_j are not themselves interpretable, and neuron-level sparsity does not yield human-readable explanations of the nonlinear interactions, only feature selection signals.

strengths: The paper is clearly written, with a coherent narrative unifying global (MEM) and local (per-instance) explanations in a single hybrid model.

The parameter elimination optimization trick (profile-likelihood style elimination of the linear coefficients, combined with adaptive ridge re-parameterization) is a clean and reasonably well-executed technical contribution, with derivations for regression, GLMs, and sub-ℓ1 pseudo-norms provided in the appendix.
An ablation study (masking the j-th feature and removing positional encoding) is included, which supports the design choices of the architecture.
Honest discussion of limitations in the conclusions (e.g., inability to capture self-interactions such as x_j f(x_j)), and acknowledgment of the ethical issues with the Boston housing dataset.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and incomplete positioning: the core idea—input-modulated linear coefficients produced by a neural network—is very close to the Contextual Lasso (Thompson et al., 2023), which the paper cites but, remarkably, never compares against experimentally. Other closely related lines (per-instance linear models, IMN) are compared only on a small subset of tasks. The paper's differentiation from the closest prior work is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The central interpretability claim is partially circular: MEM_j = β_j holds by construction of the model, not as an empirical finding. Moreover, the actual marginal effect ME_j still depends on network derivatives of the correction terms, so the 'intelligible global effect' is only valid exactly at the mean point—a point of measure zero in feature space. The claim that MEMs of other nonlinear models 'reduce to arbitrary numerical values' is an overstatement; MEM is a well-defined and meaningful quantity for any differentiable model.

The synthetic data-generating processes (Eq. 39–46) exactly match NIMO's model class (multiplicative corrections of linear coefficients), giving NIMO a structural advantage over all baselines; recovery of coefficients/nonlinearities in such tailored settings is not strong evidence of general utility.

Evaluation is narrow: only three small real datasets (442, 506, and 21k samples), a handful of synthetic settings, and no standard tabular benchmarks used in the NAM/IMN literature. Table 1 reports single numbers without error bars or significance tests; real-data results are box plots without statistical comparisons. The efficiency claim of the elimination method ('effectively and efficiently') is never supported with timing or cost analysis (the d×d linear solve per step is non-trivial for large d).

Baseline fairness concerns: baselines are largely run with default hyperparameters while NIMO uses grid search over penalties plus bespoke tricks (noise injection into the first layer, sin activations); the appendix admits 'with careful hyperparameter tuning, NIMO is capable of selecting more accurate features,' suggesting the reported results depend on tuning asymmetries.

The adaptive-ridge/Lasso equivalence proof in Appendix A is informal (e.g., it does not properly handle β_k = 0, mixes the constrained and Lagrangian forms, and treats λ inconsistently), and no convergence or consistency analysis of the overall training procedure is provided.

Several results raise doubts about robustness: NIMO selects noisy features in classification Setting 3 (acknowledged in the appendix), and the ablation shows interpretability degrades substantially without the masking trick—yet the noise-injection heuristic needed to make sparsity work is ad hoc and unexamined.
Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of any code release statement, and several figures (e.g., Figure 14 on the superconductivity dataset) are effectively unreadable at the presented scale.

strengths: The proposed model (NIMO) is simple, clearly motivated, and elegant: multiplying global linear coefficients by instance-specific neural network corrections yields a model where the marginal effect at the mean (MEM) provably coincides with the linear coefficient, providing an exact rather than approximate global interpretation.

The parameter-elimination optimization is technically sound and non-trivial: the closed-form profile solution for beta given the network parameters, the adaptive-ridge reparameterization for sparsity (with a correct proof of the adaptive-ridge/Lasso equivalence in Appendix A), and the IRLS extension to generalized linear models (logistic regression) are all well worked out.

The paper is well written and well organized, with clear distinction between local (per-instance) and global (population-level) explanations, a helpful architecture figure, and a transparent discussion of limitations (e.g., inability to capture self-interactions like x_j f(x_j)).

The empirical study covers synthetic settings with known ground truth (including sparsity recovery), three real UCI datasets, comparisons against relevant hybrid/interpretable baselines (LassoNet, NAM, IMN), and a thoughtful ablation study on feature masking and positional encoding.

The handling of the controversial 'B' feature in the Boston housing dataset, and the consistency check between SHAP rankings and MEM rankings, demonstrate a serious effort to validate interpretability claims rather than just assert them.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to closely related work. The idea of using a neural network to produce instance-specific linear coefficients is well established (varying-coefficient models, Contextual Lasso by Thompson et al. 2023, IMN by Kadra et al. 2024). NIMO's core difference is a multiplicative correction instead of directly predicting coefficients, which is an incremental architectural variation. Notably, Contextual Lasso is cited in the related work but is NOT included as an empirical baseline, which is a significant omission given it is the most directly comparable method.

The synthetic data-generating processes are of exactly the same functional form as the model class (y = sum x_j beta_j (1 + g(x_{-j}))). The recovery results in Table 1 and Figure 4 are therefore largely expected and somewhat circular; they do not test robustness to model misspecification, which is the realistic scenario.

Real-data evidence is thin: only three datasets, with NIMO merely 'compatible' with baselines on diabetes and Boston housing (not clearly better), and best only on superconductivity. No statistical significance testing is reported, and there are no high-dimensional or p >> n settings where the sparsity claims would be most compelling.

The interpretability guarantee is narrow: MEM = beta_j holds only at the mean point; the per-instance marginal effects ME_j depend on the black-box network (including cross-derivative terms), so local explanations are not themselves intelligible. The claim that MEMs computed for other nonlinear models 'reduce to arbitrary numerical values' is overstated.

Several implementation choices are heuristic and under-justified: binary positional encoding, subtracting g_u(0) to enforce the constraint, noise injection into the first layer to 'disrupt compensation' of the group penalty, and a sin activation after the second layer. The sensitivity of results to these choices is not analyzed.

There are minor inconsistencies (e.g., the loss in Algorithm 1 uses ||gamma|| while the derivation uses ||gamma||^2; a stray 'hybird' typo; Eq. 1 in the introduction differs subtly in form from Eq. 2), and no explicit code release is promised, which limits reproducibility.

The apparent gain over baselines on synthetic data may partly reflect the matched model class rather than a genuine methodological advantage; a broader empirical comparison (including Contextual Lasso, EBMs, and GAMs with pairwise interactions) is needed to support the claim of a 'favorable trade-off'.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: the architectural constraint g_uj(0)=0 with feature masking elegantly guarantees that MEM exactly equals the linear coefficient beta, unifying global and local interpretability in one model — this is a genuinely clean design.

Solid optimization contribution: parameter elimination (profile-likelihood style) with the adaptive-ridge/Lasso equivalence (proof in Appendix A) enables joint training of network parameters and linear coefficients with sparsity; extension to GLMs via IRLS is a nice bonus.

The paper is unusually honest and thorough: an explicit limitations section with a synthetic experiment showing exactly when NIMO fails (self-interactions) and how basis expansion remedies it, plus extensive ablations (masking, positional encoding, first-layer group penalty) and an additional PMLB benchmark.

Synthetic experiments convincingly demonstrate recovery of ground-truth coefficients, sparsity patterns, nonlinear corrections, and per-instance local explanations, with appropriate baselines (Lasso, NN, NAM, IMN, LassoNet) and reasonable protocol (multiple seeds, validation-based hyperparameter selection).
Related work coverage is good and the positioning against NAM, LassoNet, IMN, and IME is articulate; the distinction between global (MEM) and local explanations is well argued.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core idea of per-instance linear coefficients produced by a neural network is very close to the contextual lasso (Thompson et al., 2023), which the paper cites but does not empirically compare against. The delta over that work (masking, g(0)=0 constraint, adaptive-ridge elimination) is meaningful but incremental.

The interpretability evaluation is partly circular: since MEM = beta holds by construction, experiments showing NIMO 'accurately estimates MEM' on synthetic data largely test coefficient recovery, not the interpretability claim itself. A formal identifiability argument for beta as the true additive effect (given the network can encode interactions involving x_{-j}) is missing.

Real-data gains are modest and inconsistent: NIMO is comparable to baselines on diabetes and Boston housing and best only on superconductivity; no statistical significance testing is provided, and the interpretability comparison on real data is restricted to Lasso only — a weak comparison for a paper whose central claim is interpretability.

Scalability concerns are underexplored: the closed-form elimination requires a d x d matrix inversion per optimization step, and the paper does not quantify runtime or discuss behavior beyond 81 features.
No mention of code release, which limits reproducibility given the many implementation details (noise injection, positional encoding, sin activation) that materially affect performance.
Some claims are stated too strongly without evidence, e.g., that MEM for other nonlinear models 'reduce to arbitrary numerical values' — no empirical demonstration of this is provided.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the proposed model (Eq. 2) is simple and easy to understand; the distinction between local (per-instance correction h_j(x)) and global (MEM = β_j) effects is well articulated and Figure 1/2 communicate the idea effectively.

The optimization section is technically sound: the parameter elimination via profile likelihood, the re-parameterized adaptive ridge regression (Appendix B.1), the IRLS extension to logistic regression (B.2), and the sub-ℓ1 extension (B.3) are carefully derived, and the adaptive ridge–Lasso equivalence proof in Appendix A is correct in outline.

There is a reasonable breadth of experiments: synthetic settings with varying dimensionality and sparsity, three real UCI datasets, a classification extension, ablation studies on masking/position encoding and the group penalty, a PMLB benchmark, and an explicit limitations study (self-interactions, Sec. 4.4/D.6) — the latter is commendably honest.
The claim that MEM coincides with β is correct given the architecture, and the sanity check on the purely linear dataset (Figure 4, left) verifies that the network does not distort the linear part.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea — multiplying each feature's linear coefficient by a neural-network-derived per-instance factor — is a straightforward multiplicative gating/modulation scheme very close to existing work, notably the contextual lasso (Thompson et al., 2023, cited but not compared against) and Interpretable Mesomorphic Networks (Kadra et al., 2024, compared only on MSE). The parameter elimination trick is a standard profile-likelihood/conditional-lasso device, so the methodological contribution is incremental.

The central interpretability claim is largely tautological: MEM_j = β_j holds by construction of the architecture, not because the method discovers interpretable structure. The genuinely important question — whether β_j faithfully reflects the true data-generating feature effect — is only validated on synthetic data whose generating process exactly matches NIMO's functional form (y = Σ x_j β_j(1+g(x_-j))), which is circular and heavily favors the method over baselines.

Real-data evaluation is weak and mixed: only three small UCI datasets (442, 506, and 21k samples), 5–9 random splits with no significance testing; on diabetes NIMO is statistically indistinguishable from simpler methods, on Boston housing MEM/SHAP feature rankings are mutually inconsistent across methods (Table 2), and there is no ground truth to judge which ranking is correct. The claimed interpretability advantage is argued narratively rather than demonstrated with faithfulness metrics.

The comparison for the interpretability hypothesis (Hypothesis 2) is restricted to Lasso, which is self-serving; other interpretable baselines (NAM shape functions, IMN, LassoNet) could also provide global summaries (e.g., averaged absolute effects, ICE/PDP-based effects), and the assertion that their MEMs 'reduce to arbitrary numerical values' is asserted, not shown.

Scalability and computational cost of the elimination procedure are not analyzed: each gradient step requires solving a d×d linear system, and the practical feasibility for high-dimensional tabular problems (where interpretable models matter most) is unaddressed; the PMLB benchmark caps at 16k samples and 10 datasets, with results relegated to an appendix figure with no table or statistics.

Several design choices feel ad hoc and weakly justified: the binary positional encoding of the masked feature index, the sin activation 'to capture repeating patterns', the noise injection into the first layer to 'prevent compensation' (claimed to 'work very well in practice' without evidence beyond one ablation), and grid-search-selected penalties; sensitivity to these choices is not systematically studied.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, many undocumented implementation details (network sizes, epochs, the d networks vs. shared network inconsistency between Eq. 2/Sec. 3.1 and the abstract), and typos/figure caption errors (e.g., 'Bostong', 'hybird', broken Figure 5 caption) suggest insufficient polish.

The practical significance is unclear: on real data NIMO offers no consistent accuracy gain over a plain regularized NN, and the interpretable object (MEM = β_j) is only meaningful under the strong assumption that the true function is linear plus multiplicative corrections that exclude self-interactions — an assumption violated in many realistic settings, as the authors themselves show in D.6.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-executed: enforcing g_uj(x_{-j}) (excluding feature j from its own correction network) with g_uj(0)=0 yields the elegant property that MEM coincides exactly with the linear coefficient β_j, unifying global and local interpretability in a single architecture.

The parameter elimination / profile-likelihood optimization is a thoughtful technical contribution: closed-form elimination of β with adaptive-ridge re-parameterization enables joint training with sparsity, and the derivation is supported by a proof of the adaptive ridge–Lasso equivalence and extensions to GLMs (IRLS for logistic regression) and sub-ℓ1 pseudo-norms.

The evaluation is unusually broad and honest for this type of paper: synthetic regression and classification settings across dimensionalities, three real UCI datasets, a PMLB benchmark, ablations of masking/positional encoding/group penalty, local-explanation validation against SHAP, and an explicit limitations section (Sec. 4.4, D.6) that experimentally demonstrates where the model fails (self-interactions) and how feature engineering remedies it.
Positioning against closely related hybrid methods (NAM, LassoNet, IMN, IME) is clear, and the paper is well written with a coherent narrative from model design to interpretation to optimization.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: multiplicative input gating with a shared network, per-instance linear corrections, and context-dependent linear coefficients are closely related to existing work — the contextual lasso (Thompson et al., 2023, cited but not compared against), varying-coefficient models (Hastie & Tibshirani, 1993; not cited), and hypernetwork-based instance-wise linear models (IMN). The main differentiator (masking feature j from g_j to pin MEM = β_j) is a simple architectural constraint rather than a substantial methodological advance.

The synthetic experiments appear to be generated exactly in the model's functional form (y = Σ x_j β_j (1 + g_j(x_{-j})), e.g., Eqs. 40–47), i.e., the data-generating process matches NIMO's hypothesis class. The large MSE gaps in Table 1 (e.g., 0.024 vs. 0.078 for the next best) and perfect coefficient recovery are therefore expected and overstate the method's advantage; results on real datasets show NIMO is only comparable to (not clearly better than) baselines, with the best result on one of three datasets.

Evaluation rigor is limited: Table 1 reports single-run numbers with no standard deviations or significance tests; real-data experiments use only 5–9 splits with no statistical comparison; the PMLB benchmark is restricted to 10 datasets and includes a post-hoc basis expansion applied specifically to rescue NIMO on one dataset.

The interpretability claims deserve more scrutiny: for correlated features (acknowledged in Sec. 4.2), MEM = β_j evaluated at the (standardized) mean may not represent a meaningful population-level effect, and the local marginal effect ME_j contains cross terms Σ_{i≠j} x_i β_i ∂g/∂x_j that are not part of the proposed 'local coefficient' s_j(x) = β_j(1 + g_uj(x_{-j})) used in local explanations (Appendix D.7); the SHAP-consistency check is qualitative.

The model class is restrictive in a way that limits practical significance: NIMO cannot represent self-interactions x_j f(x_j) (even y = x² fails without feature engineering), and high-dimensional settings require solving a d×d linear system per gradient step, whose conditioning and computational cost are not analyzed.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code release is stated, and several practical ingredients (noise injection into the first layer, sin activation, positional encoding scheme, grid-search ranges) materially affect results but their sensitivity is not studied.
